usage: Polite; handing over your receipt at the counter
반말, to a friend helping you return something
Formal 합쇼체, stiffer or to a manager
Saying you have it before you hand it over
examples: 영수증 여기 있어요.
Here's the receipt.
The most basic form — said as you place the receipt on the counter; no extra words needed.
환불하려고요. 영수증 여기 있어요.
I'd like a refund. Here's the receipt.
State your purpose first, then offer proof — this sequence signals you came prepared.
A: 혹시 영수증 있으세요? / B: 네, 영수증 여기 있어요.
A: Do you happen to have the receipt? / B: Yes, here's the receipt.
Classic staff-customer exchange; B's reply is the natural beat after A's polite 있으세요? request.
nuance: 영수증 여기 있어요 is 영수증 ('receipt', Sino-Korean 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it is here / here it is'). 여기 있어요 is the natural Korean phrase for 'here you go / here it is' when presenting an object — it literally says 'it exists here', and the offering sense comes from context and gesture. Keep the receipt, because almost every Korean store requires 영수증 for a refund or exchange; without it you may only get 교환 (store exchange) or be refused entirely. The nearest near-synonym is 영수증 드릴게요 ('I'll give it to you'), which actively announces you're handing it over and feels slightly more deferential; 여기 있어요 simply presents it — both are natural, but 여기 있어요 is the everyday default. Stronger/softer variants: 영수증 여기 있습니다 (formal), 여기 있어 (반말). The English-speaker trap is translating 'here you go' word-for-word as 여기 가요, which means 'here I go / I'm going here' — the correct presenting phrase is 여기 있어요 (존재동사 있다, not 가다). A second common confusion: 영수증 (receipt, proof of payment already made) vs 계산서 (the bill/statement, often before paying) — for a return you need 영수증.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 ('receipt', 領收證) + 여기 있어요 ('it exists here'). The presenting force — 'here you go' — comes from context and gesture, not from a separate giving verb. It is the standard counter phrase when handing staff any document.

Used at any retail or service counter: refund desks, pharmacy pick-ups, parcel offices. Speech-level is 해요체 (polite-neutral). Upgrade to 여기 있습니다 (합쇼체) with a manager; drop to 여기 있어 (반말) with a friend helping you. Safe for strangers and staff.

영수증 드릴게요 ('I'll give you the receipt') actively announces the handover and is a touch more deferential; 여기 있어요 just presents it. Both are fine — 여기 있어요 is the unmarked everyday default. Distinguish 영수증 (paid receipt) from 계산서 (itemized bill, often before payment); for returns you need 영수증.
여기 있어요 → 여기 있습니다 (stiffer/formal) → 여기 있어 (반말). Add lead-in: 영수증 가지고 왔어요 ('I brought the receipt') to say you have it before presenting it.

'Here you go' → 여기 가요 is the classic trap. 가요 means 'I go/am going'; the presenting verb is 있어요 (existence). A second trap: using 계산서 instead of 영수증 for a return — 계산서 is the bill, not proof of payment.

mistakes: Saying 여기 가요 for 'here you go'.
여기 가요 means 'I'm going here / here I go', not 'here it is'. To present an object, say 여기 있어요 — the existence verb 있다, not the motion verb 가다.
Confusing 영수증 with 계산서.
영수증 is the receipt (proof you paid); 계산서 is the bill/itemized statement before paying. For a refund or exchange the staff want the 영수증.
Attempting a return with no receipt and expecting a full refund.
Most Korean stores require 영수증 for a cash refund; without it you may get only 교환 (exchange) or store credit. Keep and present it: 영수증 여기 있어요.

english: Can I get a refund on this?
usage: Can I get a refund on this?
Polite-neutral; asking if a refund is possible
반말, to a friendly small-shop owner
Is a refund possible for this?
가능하다 ('to be possible'), a common interchangeable form
examples: 이거 환불돼요?
Can I get a refund on this?
Your opening move — check feasibility before making any demand; holding the item as you ask.
영수증 있는데, 이거 환불돼요?
I have the receipt — can I get a refund on this?
Lead with 영수증 있는데 to signal you're prepared; 있는데 sets up a contrast ('I have it, so…').
A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 이거 한 번도 안 썼는데 환불돼요?
A: How can I help you? / B: I never used this — can I get a refund?
A is the typical staff opener; B answers with the reason + question, the natural real-world two-turn sequence.
nuance: 이거 환불돼요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불 ('refund', Sino-Korean 還拂) + 되다 ('to be done/possible') in polite question form — 'is a refund possible for this?'. The 되다 frames it as checking feasibility, which is exactly right as your opening move: you ask IF a refund is possible before you ask them to actually carry it out. Once they confirm it can be done, you follow with the request 환불해 주세요. Distinguish three near-synonyms by scope: 이거 환불돼요? is about one item right now; 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks about the store's general policy; 환불해 주세요 is the actual request to do it. Also keep clear the meaning trio: 환불 (money back) vs 교환 (different item) vs 반품 (physically returning the goods). The English-speaker error is over-translating 'can I' as a permission/ability question: 제가 환불할 수 있어요? sounds like YOU are asking whether you have the ability to issue a refund — backwards. The passive feasibility form 되다 is idiomatic: 환불돼요?. Another trap is the particle: 이거를 환불돼요? is wrong because 되다 here is intransitive — no object particle on 이거.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 환불(還拂) + 되다 → 'is a refund doable/possible for this?'. 되다 is intransitive feasibility, not a transitive action. This is a feasibility check, not a request — the request comes after: 환불해 주세요.

Your very first line at the counter before stating your reason. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — safe with all staff. In a tiny market 환불돼? (반말) is possible with a familiar owner. Do not use this in writing; in a customer-service chat, 환불 가능한가요? is more formal.
환불돼요? (this item, right now) vs 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? (the store's general policy) vs 환불해 주세요 (actual request). Also: 환불 (money back) ≠ 교환 (swap item) ≠ 반품 (send it back).
환불돼요? → 환불 되나요? (softer) → 환불 가능해요? (near-synonym) → 환불 가능한가요? (formal/written). Lead-in: 한 번도 안 썼는데 환불돼요? ('never used it — refundable?').

'Can I' → 제가 환불할 수 있어요? implies YOUR ability to issue a refund — backwards. Use the passive feasibility form 되다: 환불돼요?. Also: 이거를 환불돼요? is wrong — 되다 is intransitive here, so no object particle on 이거.

mistakes: Saying 제가 환불할 수 있어요? to ask for a refund.
That asks about your own ability to issue a refund and sounds backwards. Use the passive feasibility form: 이거 환불돼요? ('can this be refunded?').
Confusing 환불 with 교환 or 반품.
환불 = money back; 교환 = swap for another item; 반품 = returning the goods. If you want your money, ask 환불돼요?, not 교환돼요?.
Adding an object particle: 이거를 환불돼요?.
되다 ('to be possible') is intransitive here, so there's no object particle. Say 이거 환불돼요? — bare 이거.

usage: Polite; the standard request to be refunded
반말, to a friend or very casual seller
Could you give me a refund, please?
I'd like to request a refund
Softer, deferential with 부탁드리다 ('to request a favor')
examples: 환불해 주세요.
Please give me a refund.
Said once you've confirmed a refund is possible and shown the receipt — this is your actual request.
사이즈가 안 맞아서요. 환불해 주세요.
The size doesn't fit — please refund it.
Give the reason with -아서요 first, then the request; this soft reason-first structure is natural Korean complaint phrasing.
A: 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 이거 카드로 결제했는데 환불해 주세요.
A: How would you like to proceed? / B: I paid for this by card — please refund it.
B mentions payment method so staff refund to the right channel (card, not cash); the A/B format mirrors a real service-desk exchange.
nuance: 환불해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 해 주세요 ('please do for me', from 해 주다, the favor-verb pattern). The 해 주다 is what turns it into a courteous request for the staff's help rather than a flat command: bare 환불하세요 would be an order ('you refund!'), which sounds bossy and rude. Use this AFTER you've confirmed a refund is possible with 환불돼요?; if you jump straight to 환불해 주세요 without the preamble, it can seem aggressive. 환불 is a 하다-noun — it needs the verb 하다, so you cannot say 환불 주세요 ('please give a refund') as though 환불 is a physical object you can hand over. To de-escalate when staff resist, soften to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요. Korean law requires card purchases to be refunded back to the same card (카드 취소), not in cash — always mention 카드로 결제했어요 so staff process it correctly. The English-speaker error is the missing favor verb (환불하세요, too blunt) or the ungrammatical 환불 주세요. Another pitfall is register mismatch: 환불 부탁드립니다 in a casual market stall sounds oddly stiff, while plain 환불 in a department store sounds rude — default to 환불해 주세요 and calibrate.

structuredNuance.t: 환불(還拂) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). Literally 'please do the refund for me' — the favor-verb 주다 signals a polite request for the other person's help, not a command. Use AFTER confirming 환불돼요? — this is the execution step.

Stage two at the counter — after feasibility is confirmed. 해요체 (polite-neutral) with all staff. Upgrade to 환불해 주시겠어요? or 환불 부탁드려요 if the clerk is reluctant or you're at a formal department-store service desk. Do not use bare 환불하세요 — it is imperative and rude to staff.

환불해 주세요 (general request, any stage) vs 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 (specifically 'please execute/process it now', once agreed). 환불 부탁드려요 is softer and more face-saving when staff are reluctant. 환불 주세요 is wrong — 환불 is not a physical object you can give.
환불해 주세요 → 환불해 주시겠어요? → 환불 부탁드려요 → 환불 부탁드립니다 (most formal). Casual: 환불해 줘 (반말). Add reason: 사이즈가 안 맞아서 환불해 주세요.

Two errors: (1) 환불하세요 — the bare imperative is a command, not a request; add 주세요. (2) 환불 주세요 — 환불 is a 하다-noun and can't be 'given'; it needs 하다: 환불해 주세요. Also: card refunds go back to the card (카드 취소), not in cash — state your payment method.

mistakes: Saying 환불하세요 to the staff.
Bare 환불하세요 is an imperative ('you, refund!') and sounds commanding. The polite favor form is 환불해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Saying 환불 주세요 without 하다.
환불 is a 하다-noun and can't be 'given' directly. It needs 하다 + the favor 주다: 환불해 주세요, not 환불 주세요.
Demanding cash back for a card purchase.
By card you're refunded to the same card, not in cash (카드 결제는 카드로 환불). Say 카드로 결제했어요, 환불해 주세요, and expect the card to be credited.

usage: Polite; stating you want to swap the item
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Asking first whether an exchange is possible
examples: 이거 교환하고 싶어요.
I'd like to exchange this.
Stated while presenting the item; combines purpose with politeness — no need to explain yet.
사이즈가 작아서 한 치수 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
It's too small, so I'd like to exchange it for one size up.
한 치수 큰 걸로 ('for one size up') specifies exactly what you want; -아서 gives the reason without sounding accusatory.
A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 색깔이 마음에 안 들어서 교환하고 싶은데요.
A: How can I help? / B: I don't like the colour, so I'd like an exchange.
B uses the soft -ㄴ데요 ender, which is warmer than a flat statement and naturally invites the staff to respond.
nuance: 교환하고 싶어요 is 교환 ('exchange', Sino-Korean 交換) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'), 'I want to exchange (this)'. Unlike ordering food — where 먹고 싶어요 can sound bluntly desire-focused — for returns and exchanges 하고 싶어요 is perfectly polite, because you're stating your purpose to staff who'll then guide you. Many Korean learners soften this further to 교환하고 싶은데요… (trailing -ㄴ데요) to invite the staff's response. The crucial distinction: 교환돼요? checks IF an exchange is possible; 교환하고 싶어요 declares that you WANT one — always check first if unsure. Know the three-way split: 교환 (swap for another item) vs 환불 (money back) vs 반품 (physically sending back the goods). When naming the replacement, use -로/-으로: 큰 사이즈로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. The English-speaker error is confusing 교환 with 변경 ('change/alter', used for reservations, plans, or settings) — you 교환 a product but 변경 a booking. Forgetting -로/-으로 on the replacement target makes the request vague: 큰 거 교환 is incomplete; 큰 걸로 교환 is correct.

structuredNuance.t: 교환(交換) + 하고 싶어요 → 'I want to do an exchange'. The -고 싶어요 desire form is entirely natural here; staff read it as a polite statement of purpose, not a brash want. Softening option: 교환하고 싶은데요… (trailing -ㄴ데요).
Said at the counter when you want a different item, not a refund. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Can say it to any staff member. If you haven't yet confirmed an exchange is allowed, open with 교환돼요? first.
교환하고 싶어요 (want an exchange) vs 교환돼요? (is it possible?) vs 환불해 주세요 (want money back) vs 반품하고 싶어요 (want to physically return the goods). 교환 ≠ 변경 — 변경 is for reservations/plans/settings, not products.
교환하고 싶어요 → 교환하고 싶은데요… → 교환하려고요 ('I'm here to exchange'). Add target with -로: 큰 사이즈로 교환하고 싶어요 / 다른 색으로 교환해 주세요.
두 함정: (1) 교환 vs 변경 — products use 교환, reservations/plans use 변경. (2) Missing -로/-으로 on the target: 큰 거 교환 is vague; 큰 걸로 교환 ('exchange for a big one') is the correct form marking what you swap INTO.

mistakes: Using 변경하고 싶어요 to swap a product.
변경 is for changing plans, reservations, or settings; a physical product swap is 교환. Say 교환하고 싶어요, not 변경하고 싶어요.
Forgetting -로/-으로 on the replacement.
To name what you're swapping for, use -로: 큰 걸로 교환, 다른 색으로 교환. Without it (큰 거 교환) the target item is unclear.
Saying 교환하고 싶어요 when you actually want money back.
교환 gets you a different item, not cash. If you want your money, say 환불해 주세요, not 교환하고 싶어요.

english: Please swap it for a different one
usage: Please swap it for a different one
Polite; asking to exchange for another item
Swap it for a different one
반말, to a friend or casual stall
Could you swap it for a different one?
Please swap it for a different color
다른 색으로 ('for a different color') when only the color is off
examples: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Please swap this for a different one.
The everyday counter request when the item itself is fine but you want a clean replacement.
이거 흠집 있어서 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
This has a scratch — please swap it for a different one.
흠집 있다 ('has a scratch') names the defect; -아서 links reason to request without hostility.
A: 뭐가 문제예요? / B: 여기 실밥 풀렸어요. 같은 걸로 새 거 있으면 바꿔 주세요.
A: What's the problem? / B: The stitching came loose here. If you have a new one of the same, please swap it.
B points to the exact flaw (실밥 풀리다 = stitching unraveled), then qualifies with 새 거 있으면, making the request realistic.
nuance: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 is 다른 ('different/other') + 걸로 (걸 = 거 'thing' + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please change it for me'). 바꾸다 is the native Korean verb 'to change/swap', warmer and more everyday than the Sino-Korean 교환하다 — both work at a counter, but 바꿔 주세요 is what most people say naturally. The -로 on 다른 걸로 is essential: it marks the target you're swapping INTO ('for a different one'); drop it and 다른 거 바꿔 주세요 sounds incomplete. The dividing line from 환불해 주세요 is outcome: 바꿔 주세요 gets you a replacement item; 환불해 주세요 gets you your money back. Specify what's wrong or what you want (다른 색으로, 큰 사이즈로, 새 걸로) so staff know whether it's a defect swap or a preference swap. The English-speaker error is saying 다른 거 주세요 ('give me a different one') without the exchange framing — that sounds like you're starting a fresh purchase, not swapping the item you hold. Another pitfall: 바꾸다 works for physical items; don't use it for changing a reservation (use 변경하다) or changing money (use 환전하다).

structuredNuance.t: 다른 ('different') + 걸로 (thing + -로 'into/for') + 바꿔 주세요 ('please swap for me'). 바꾸다 is native Korean for 'swap/change'; -로 marks the target. Without -로, the sentence is incomplete.

Used when you want a physical replacement, not a refund. Natural at any retail counter. 해요체 (polite-neutral). With a manager or when being persistent, upgrade to 다른 걸로 바꿔 주시겠어요?. Dropping to 바꿔 줘 (반말) is only for close friends or an unusually casual seller.

바꿔 주세요 (swap item, native verb, warm) vs 교환해 주세요 (exchange, Sino-Korean, slightly more formal) — both get you a replacement. Neither returns money: for money back, say 환불해 주세요. 다른 거 주세요 (just 'give me a different one') has no exchange framing and sounds like a new purchase.
다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요 → 큰 사이즈로 바꿔 주세요 → 새 걸로 바꿔 주세요 → 같은 거 새 걸로 바꿔 주세요. The -로 slot accepts any target: 다른 색으로, 다른 사이즈로.
Saying 다른 거 주세요 sounds like a new purchase, not an exchange. The swap framing requires 바꿔: 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요. Also: 바꾸다 is for physical items; reservations use 변경하다, currency exchange uses 환전하다.

mistakes: Dropping -로 and saying 다른 거 바꿔 주세요.
The -로 marks what you swap INTO; without it the sentence dangles. Say 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Saying 다른 거 주세요 to mean 'exchange this'.
That sounds like asking for a different item as a new request, not swapping the one you hold. For an exchange, use 바꿔 주세요: 이거 다른 걸로 바꿔 주세요.
Using 바꿔 주세요 when you want money back.
바꾸다 swaps one item for another; it doesn't return money. If you want a refund, say 환불해 주세요.

usage: Polite; flagging a faulty product gently
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Flat statement, a touch more direct
I think it's a defective item
examples: 이거 불량인데요.
This one's defective.
Said while showing the faulty item to staff; the trailing -ㄴ데요 invites their response rather than accusing.
새로 샀는데 이거 불량인데요. 작동이 안 돼요.
I just bought it, but it's defective — it doesn't work.
작동이 안 되다 ('doesn't operate') names the specific malfunction; saying 새로 샀는데 heads off any suggestion you broke it through use.
A: 어디가 문제예요? / B: 박스 열자마자 봤는데 이거 불량인데요. 사진 찍어 뒀어요.
A: What's the problem? / B: I noticed it the moment I opened the box — this is defective. I took photos.
B's 박스 열자마자 ('the instant I opened the box') makes a strong case that the defect is pre-existing, not user-caused; 사진 찍어 뒀어요 offers proof.
nuance: 이거 불량인데요 is 이거 ('this') + 불량 ('defect/defective', Sino-Korean 不良) + 인데요 (copula 이다 + soft ender -ㄴ데요). 불량 means the product is functionally faulty from the maker — a manufacturing defect — and 불량품 is the noun form 'a defective item'. The -ㄴ데요 ender is the politeness engine: it raises the problem as 'here's the situation…' and invites the staff to respond, so it's far gentler than a flat 이거 불량이에요, which can sound like an accusation. The dividing line from 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) is function vs condition: 불량 implies it doesn't work right (functional fault), while 하자 is a visible blemish — a scratch, crack, or tear. For electronics that won't turn on, 불량 fits; for a visible blemish on packaging, 하자 있어요 is more precise. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'broken' and saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new item — 고장 implies it broke down after some use, whereas a product faulty out of the box is 불량. Note: 불량 is also slang for a 'delinquent person' (불량 학생), but with a product it unambiguously means defective.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 불량(不良) + 인데요 → 'this is [a case of] poor quality / defective — here's the situation'. 불량 = a manufacturing fault (functional). The -ㄴ데요 ender softens the claim into a situation-framer that invites the staff's response, rather than a blunt accusation.

Used when a brand-new item doesn't function correctly. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — appropriate with all staff. Softer option: 불량품인 것 같아요 (hedge with 것 같다). Point at the defect as you speak to make it concrete. Avoid being in 반말 with staff even if frustrated.

불량 (functional fault, from factory) vs 하자 (blemish/flaw in condition: scratch, crack, tear) vs 고장 (breakdown after some use). For a never-worked item: 불량. For a visible mark: 하자 있어요. For a phone that stopped working after a week: 고장 났어요.
이거 불량인데요 (soft) → 이거 불량이에요 (direct) → 불량품인 것 같아요 (hedged) → 불량품이에요 (noun form). Escalate: 불량품이라서 교환해 주세요 / 환불해 주세요.

'Broken' → 고장났어요 is wrong for a brand-new faulty item. 고장 = broke down after use; 불량 = defective from the start. Also: 불량 is also slang for a delinquent person, but in a product context it always means defective.

mistakes: Saying 고장났어요 for a brand-new faulty item.
고장 means it broke down (usually after use). A product faulty from the start is 불량: 이거 불량인데요 / 불량품이에요.
Dropping -ㄴ데요 and stating flat 이거 불량이에요.
The bare statement can sound accusatory. The soft ender raises it gently: 이거 불량인데요 lets staff respond without feeling blamed.
Confusing 불량 (faulty function) with 하자 (blemish/flaw).
불량 = doesn't work right; 하자 = a flaw like a scratch or crack. For a non-working item say 불량, for a visible blemish say 하자 있어요.

usage: Polite; pointing out a blemish on the product
반말, to a friend or casual seller
흠집 ('scratch') for a surface mark specifically
It seems to have a bit of a flaw
examples: 여기 하자 있어요.
There's a flaw here.
Said while pointing directly at the blemish — the 여기 + gesture combination makes the complaint concrete and hard to dismiss.
여기 보세요, 하자 있어요. 박음질이 터졌어요.
Look here — there's a flaw. The stitching's come apart.
박음질이 터지다 ('the stitching burst') names the exact defect; 보세요 invites the staff to verify rather than just trust your word.
A: 언제 발견하셨어요? / B: 살 때는 몰랐는데 집에서 보니까 여기 하자 있어요.
A: When did you notice? / B: I didn't see it when buying, but at home I noticed a flaw here.
B's 집에서 보니까 explains why it wasn't caught in-store, making the late complaint more credible.
nuance: 여기 하자 있어요 is 여기 ('here') + 하자 ('flaw/blemish', Sino-Korean 瑕疵) + 있어요 ('there is'). 하자 is the precise term for a defect in condition — a scratch, crack, tear, stain, or other blemish — as opposed to 불량, which leans toward a functional fault (it doesn't work). Pointing with 여기 ('here') as you say it makes the complaint concrete and helps staff see exactly what you mean. For an everyday surface mark, the native 흠집 ('scratch/nick') is even more specific: 여기 흠집 났어요. The dividing line: 하자 있어요 is calm and somewhat formal (it's the word used in warranties and consumer-protection law), 흠집 났어요 is plainer and very visual, while 불량이에요 says the thing fails to function. The English-speaker error is using 'have' literally and saying 이거 하자를 가지고 있어요 — Korean expresses 'there is a flaw' with the existence verb 있다, not 가지다; say 하자 있어요. Another pitfall is the particle: 하자 있어요 (or 하자가 있어요), never 하자를 있어요 — 있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Pair it with a defect word (터지다 'burst', 깨지다 'cracked', 찢어지다 'torn') to be unambiguous.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 ('here') + 하자(瑕疵, 'flaw/blemish') + 있어요 ('there is'). The existence verb 있다 is what 'there is a flaw' maps to in Korean — not 가지다 ('have/possess'). Pointing as you speak makes the complaint specific and hard to argue with.

Used at a counter or on the phone when reporting a visible defect: scratch, crack, tear, stain. 해요체 (polite-neutral). 하자 is also the term used in consumer-protection policies, so staff recognize it immediately. For a casual market, 여기 흠집 났어요 (native word) is equally natural.

하자 있어요 (formal, in policies/law, blemish in condition) vs 흠집 났어요 (native, 'got scratched', very visual) vs 불량이에요 (functional fault — won't work). Don't use 하자 for things that simply don't function: that's 불량 or 고장.
여기 하자 있어요 → 여기 하자가 있어요 (subject particle added, same meaning) → 하자가 좀 있는 것 같은데요 (hedged). Add specifics: 여기 깨져 있어요 (cracked), 여기 찢어져 있어요 (torn), 여기 흠집 났어요 (scratched).
Two errors: (1) 하자를 가지고 있어요 ('it possesses a flaw') — use the existence verb: 하자 있어요. (2) Particle error: 하자를 있어요 is wrong; 있다 takes the subject particle 이/가, not the object particle 을/를.

mistakes: Saying 하자를 가지고 있어요.
Korean uses the existence verb for 'there is a flaw': 하자 있어요, not the 'possess' verb 가지다. 가지고 있어요 sounds like a translation of English 'have'.
Using 하자를 있어요 with the object particle.
있다 takes 이/가, not 을/를. Say 하자 있어요 or 하자가 있어요, never 하자를 있어요.
Using 하자 for something that simply doesn't work.
하자 is a blemish/flaw in condition. If the item won't function at all, that's 불량 or 고장 — say 작동이 안 돼요 or 불량이에요.

usage: This is broken / It broke down
Polite; reporting that something stopped working
반말, to a friend or casual seller
It doesn't work / won't turn on
Describing the symptom instead of naming 'broken'
examples: 이거 고장 났어요.
This is broken.
Said while showing the device that won't work; clear, matter-of-fact, no blame implied.
산 지 일주일밖에 안 됐는데 고장 났어요.
It's only been a week since I bought it, and it broke.
산 지 일주일밖에 안 됐다 emphasizes how recently it was bought, implying the fault isn't from extended use.
A: 어디가 안 되세요? / B: 전원이 안 켜져요. 이거 고장 난 것 같아요.
A: What seems to be the problem? / B: It won't power on. I think it's broken.
B describes the symptom (전원이 안 켜지다 'won't power on') before naming 고장, which helps staff diagnose before asserting a defect.
nuance: 이거 고장 났어요 is 이거 ('this') + 고장 ('breakdown/malfunction', Sino-Korean 故障) + 났어요 (past of 나다, here 'to occur/arise'). The fixed collocation is 고장이 나다 — literally 'a breakdown occurs' — so 'it's broken' comes out as 고장 났어요, NOT 고장했어요 (고장 is not a 하다-verb) or 고장됐어요. This phrasing is for machines, devices, and appliances that stop working. The dividing line from 불량 is timing/cause: 고장 means it broke down, usually after some use, while 불량 means it was faulty from the factory; a phone that worked for a week and then died can use either depending on emphasis, but a never-worked item leans 불량. Don't apply 고장 to non-mechanical 'broken': a cracked screen is 깨졌어요; a torn bag is 찢어졌어요; a snapped cable is 끊어졌어요; a broken zipper is 지퍼가 고장 났어요 or 지퍼가 안 잠겨요. The English-speaker error is the wrong verb pairing: 고장했어요 or 고장됐어요 are not standard; the correct pairing is 고장 + 나다. Another pitfall is using 고장 for a torn or shattered item — those use different Korean verbs.

structuredNuance.t: 고장(故障) + 났어요 ('occurred/arose') → 'a breakdown occurred'. 고장 is a noun; it collocates with 나다, not 하다 or 되다. Think of it as 'a malfunction happened' rather than 'it did a breakdown'.

For machines, electronics, appliances — things that stop functioning. Not for physical breakage (snapping, shattering). 해요체 (polite-neutral). When unsure, describe the symptom instead: 작동이 안 돼요 / 전원이 안 켜져요.
고장 났어요 (machine broke down after use) vs 불량이에요 (faulty from the factory) vs 작동이 안 돼요 (symptom description: doesn't operate). For physical damage: 깨졌어요 (shattered), 찢어졌어요 (torn), 부러졌어요 (snapped).
이거 고장 났어요 → 고장 난 것 같아요 (hedged) → 고장이 난 건 아닌데 작동이 안 돼요 (softer: 'not sure it's broken but it won't work'). Also: 고장 수리 맡기다 ('send for repair'), A/S 신청하다 ('apply for after-sales service').
고장했어요 and 고장됐어요 are both wrong — 고장 pairs with 나다. Say 고장 났어요. Also: 고장 is only for machines; for a torn/shattered/snapped item use the correct breakage verb (깨지다, 찢어지다, 부러지다).

mistakes: Saying 고장했어요 or 고장됐어요.
고장 pairs with the verb 나다: the correct form is 고장 났어요 ('a breakdown occurred'). 고장하다/고장되다 are not standard.
Using 고장 for non-machines.
고장 is for devices/machinery. A snapped pencil is 부러졌어요, shattered glass is 깨졌어요, a torn bag is 찢어졌어요 — not 고장 났어요.
Confusing 고장 (broke down) with 불량 (faulty from the start).
If it worked then failed, 고장 났어요; if it never worked out of the box, 불량이에요. Pick based on whether it ever functioned.

usage: Polite-neutral; asking how returns work here
반말, to a friend who works there
How does the refund policy work?
환불 정책 ('refund policy'), a near-synonym of 규정
examples: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?
What's the refund policy?
Asked before buying — the smartest time, since you'll know your options before any problem arises.
혹시 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? 며칠 안에 가능한가요?
What's the refund policy — how many days do I have?
혹시 ('by any chance') softens the inquiry; 며칠 안에 가능한가요? drills down to the time limit immediately.
A: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / B: 7일 이내에 영수증 지참하시면 가능해요.
A: What's the refund policy? / B: Within 7 days with the receipt, it's possible.
B's reply is the typical staff formula — 이내에 ('within'), 영수증 지참 ('with receipt in hand'); learning this means you'll understand the answer too.
nuance: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? is 환불 ('refund') + 규정 ('regulation/policy', Sino-Korean 規定) + 이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it go / what is it?'). The set frame …이/가 어떻게 돼요? is the natural Korean way to ask 'what is X / how does X work' for policies, fees, schedules, and personal details — it's softer and more conversational than a blunt 뭐예요?. This question asks the store to explain its full return rules: time limits, receipt requirements, sale-item exclusions. The dividing line from 환불돼요? is scope: 환불돼요? is about one specific item right now; 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks for the store's general policy. 규정 and 정책 are interchangeable here, with 규정 sounding slightly more like 'the official rules'. The English-speaker error is translating 'what is the policy' as 환불 규정이 뭐예요? — grammatically possible but blunt and survey-like; natives prefer the 어떻게 돼요? frame. The particle trap: 규정이 어떻게 돼요 (subject particle 이), never 규정을 어떻게 돼요. Mastering 어떻게 돼요? unlocks many polite info questions: 가격이 어떻게 돼요? (price), 영업시간이 어떻게 돼요? (hours).

structuredNuance.t: 환불 + 규정(規定, 'regulation/policy') + 이 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it become?'). 어떻게 돼요? is a versatile information frame meaning 'what/how is X' — softer than 뭐예요?, more open-ended than a yes/no. It asks staff to explain the full policy.

Ask before buying (ideally) or before the return attempt. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — correct with all staff. In writing/email, 환불 규정이 어떻게 되나요? or 환불 정책을 안내해 주시겠어요? is more formal. Don't use 반말 with staff.
환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? (general policy, open) vs 이거 환불돼요? (this one specific item, closed yes/no) vs 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (the time-limit sub-question). 규정 ≈ 정책 in this context — both natural.
어떻게 돼요? transfers across topics: 교환 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / 반품 규정이 어떻게 돼요? / 가격이 어떻게 돼요?. For a specific follow-up: 며칠 이내예요? ('within how many days?').
환불 규정이 뭐예요? is grammatically fine but sounds abrupt — use 어떻게 돼요?. Particle error: 규정을 어떻게 돼요? is wrong; 되다 takes the subject particle: 규정이 어떻게 돼요?.

mistakes: Asking 환불 규정이 뭐예요?.
Grammatically fine but abrupt and survey-like. The natural, polite frame is 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?.
Using the object particle: 환불 규정을 어떻게 돼요?.
되다 takes the subject particle here: 환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요?. 규정을 is wrong with 되다.
Confusing the general policy with one item.
환불 규정이 어떻게 돼요? asks the overall rules. To ask about the specific thing in your hand, say 이거 환불돼요?.

english: By how many days do I have to get a refund?
usage: Within how many days do I have to refund it?
How many days do I have to refund?
반말, to a friend or casual seller
How many days is the refund window?
환불 기간 ('refund period'), asking the window directly
Until when is a refund possible?
언제까지 ('by when'), asking the cutoff date
examples: 이거 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요?
By how many days do I have to get this refunded?
The smart follow-up to ask at the moment of buying so you know your exact deadline before any problem arises.
며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? 일주일 지나면 안 돼요?
How many days do I have? Is it no good after a week?
일주일 지나면 ('if a week passes') probes the boundary; this two-beat structure is natural in real negotiation.
A: 선물할 건데요, 혹시 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? / B: 14일 이내에 영수증 있으시면 가능해요.
A: I'm buying this as a gift — within how many days must it be refunded? / B: Within 14 days, with the receipt.
A's 선물할 건데요 explains why the window matters; B's reply gives the standard Korean policy formula — 14일 이내, 영수증.
nuance: 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? is 며칠 ('how many days') + 안에 ('within') + 환불하다 ('to refund') + -아야 되다 ('have to / must'). The core grammar -아/어야 되다 expresses obligation or a deadline: 'within how many days must the refund be done?'. 안에 ('within') takes a time noun directly: 일주일 안에, 14일 안에, 한 달 안에. Korean stores typically allow returns within 7 or 14 days (7일/14일 이내), so knowing this is genuinely practical. The dividing line from 환불 기간이 며칠이에요? ('how long is the refund period?') is angle: 며칠 안에 …해야 돼요? frames it as your obligation/deadline, while 환불 기간 asks for the policy window as a plain fact — both yield the same answer. Two spelling traps for English speakers: 며칠 ('how many days', one word) is often misspelled 몇 일 even by native speakers; the correct spelling is 며칠 — write it as one word. Second: 안에 ('within') and 안 ('not') look similar but are entirely different — 며칠 안에 = 'within how many days'; 안 would negate a verb. The obligation ending is 돼요 (from 되다), not 해요, so 환불해야 돼요?, not 환불해야 해요? (though -아야 하다 is also used in formal contexts).

structuredNuance.t: 며칠 ('how many days') + 안에 ('within') + 환불해야 ('must refund') + 돼요? → 'within how many days must the refund happen?'. Frames it as your obligation/deadline — subtly implying you want to comply, which is politer than demanding to know if you can still get one.

Ask at point of purchase, not when you already have a problem. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Gifts and online orders especially warrant this question. If you've missed the window, it's better to ask 지금도 환불 가능한가요? ('is a refund still possible?') rather than this form.

며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요? (deadline as obligation) vs 환불 기간이 며칠이에요? (window as fact) vs 언제까지 환불 가능해요? (cutoff date). All three ask for the same information from different angles — 며칠 안에 is the most natural spoken form.
-아야 되다 transfers: 교환해야 돼요? (exchange deadline), 반품해야 돼요? (return deadline). Also: 며칠 이내예요? ('within how many days?', shorter). The time noun slot: 며칠 / 일주일 / 14일 / 한 달.

두 함정: (1) 며칠 spelling — the correct form is 며칠, NOT 몇 일; even many native speakers misspell this. (2) 안에 vs 안 — 안에 = 'within' (a time/space frame); 안 = 'not' (negation). They look similar but are unrelated.

mistakes: Spelling it 몇 일 안에.
The question word for 'how many days' is written 며칠, one word — not 몇 일. So it's 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요?.
Confusing 안에 ('within') with 안 ('not').
안에 sets a time/space frame ('within'); 안 negates a verb. 며칠 안에 = 'within how many days'; 며칠 안 환불해요 would be nonsense.
Mixing up 얼마 안에 and 며칠 안에.

얼마 안에 means 'within a short while' (vague); the correct deadline question word is 며칠 ('how many days'): 며칠 안에 환불해야 돼요?. Saying 얼마 안에 환불해야 돼요? asks 'must I refund within a short time?' rather than asking how many days.

usage: Polite; sending an item back (esp. online orders)
반말, to a friend or casual seller
반품하려고요 ('intending to return it'), softer announcement
반품 신청 ('return application'), the online/app step
examples: 이거 반품하고 싶어요.
I'd like to return this.
In a physical store, stating your purpose clearly at the start; staff will then guide you through the process.
온라인에서 샀는데 반품하고 싶어요. 어떻게 해요?
I bought it online — I'd like to return it. How do I do that?
온라인에서 샀다 ('bought online') is key context since the process (app, courier) differs from in-store.
A: 네, 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 마음에 안 들어서 반품하고 싶은데, 택배비는 누가 내요?
A: How can I help you? / B: I don't like it and want to return it — who pays the shipping?
B immediately asks the critical online-return question: 택배비 누가 내요? ('who pays shipping?'). The answer depends on 단순 변심 (buyer pays) vs 불량 (seller pays).
nuance: 이거 반품하고 싶어요 is 이거 ('this') + 반품 ('returning goods', Sino-Korean 返品) + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'). 반품 is specifically the act of sending the product back — the physical/logistical return — which then results in a 환불 (refund) or sometimes 교환 (exchange). This word dominates online shopping, where you 반품 신청 ('file a return request') through an app and arrange for a courier pickup. The three-way distinction: 반품 = give the goods back physically; 환불 = get your money back; 교환 = swap for another item. They're related but not interchangeable: saying 환불하고 싶어요 when the agent needs to arrange a courier pickup can confuse things. For online 단순 변심 ('simple change of mind') returns you pay return shipping 택배비; for 불량 ('defect') returns the seller typically pays — always ask 택배비는 누가 내요?. Don't confuse 반품 with 반납 ('returning something borrowed or rented', like a library book or a rental car) — you 반품 a purchase but 반납 a rental. For in-store, 반품 works, but people often just say 환불해 주세요 directly.

structuredNuance.t: 반품(返品) = 'returning goods' + 하고 싶어요 ('want to do'). 반품 is the logistics of sending the product back — it's the first step; 환불 (money) or 교환 (replacement) is the result. Dominant in online commerce; in-store people often skip to 환불해 주세요.

Use when the item actually needs to go back — especially for online orders where a courier must be arranged. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Online: 반품 신청하다 (apply through the app). In-store: 반품하고 싶어요 or 환불해 주세요. Always ask 택배비 누가 내요? for online returns.
반품하고 싶어요 (send the item back, logistics) vs 환불해 주세요 (get money back) vs 교환하고 싶어요 (swap for different item). 반품 ≠ 반납 — 반납 is for borrowed/rented items (도서관 책 반납, 렌터카 반납).
반품하고 싶어요 → 반품하려고요 (softer announcement) → 반품 신청할게요 ('I'll file a return request', online). Lead-in: 단순 변심인데 반품하고 싶어요 / 불량인데 반품하고 싶어요 (state reason, as it affects shipping cost).

'Return' maps to both 반품 and 환불 in English — but they are different steps in Korean. 반품 is the physical return; 환불 is the money. Mixing them can cause confusion. Also: 반납 (return a rental/borrowed item) ≠ 반품 (return a purchase). For 단순 변심 online returns, you (the buyer) pay 택배비.

mistakes: Using 환불 when you mean sending the item back.
환불 is the money refund; the act of returning the goods is 반품. For online orders especially, say 반품하고 싶어요, then sort out the 환불.
Confusing 반품 (return a purchase) with 반납 (return a rental/borrowed item).
반품 is for goods you bought; 반납 is for things you borrowed or rented (books, equipment). Don't say 반납하고 싶어요 for a store purchase.
Forgetting to ask about 택배비 (shipping) on online returns.
For 단순 변심 ('change of mind') the buyer usually pays return shipping; for 불량 ('defect') the seller does. Ask 택배비는 누가 내요? when you say 반품하고 싶어요.

english: Can I get a refund even without the receipt?
usage: Can I refund it even without the receipt?
Is there no refund without a receipt?
Phrased as 'won't it work without one?'
Do I absolutely need the receipt?
Asking directly if the receipt is mandatory
examples: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요?
Can I get a refund even without the receipt?
When you've lost or thrown away the receipt; the -도 ('even') acknowledges you know it's normally required.
영수증을 잃어버렸는데, 영수증 없이도 환불돼요?
I lost the receipt — can I still get a refund?
영수증을 잃어버리다 ('lost the receipt') explains the situation upfront, making the follow-up question less awkward.
A: 영수증 있으세요? / B: 카드로 샀는데 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? 카드 내역 있잖아요.
A: Do you have the receipt? / B: I paid by card — can I refund without the receipt? There's a card record.
B pivots to 카드 내역 (card transaction record) as an alternative to the receipt — this often works and is a genuinely useful tactic.
nuance: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? is 영수증 ('receipt') + 없이 ('without', the adverb derived from 없다) + -도 ('even/also') + 환불돼요? ('is a refund possible?'). The key element is 없이도 — 없이 means 'without', and -도 adds 'even', so together it asks 'is a refund possible EVEN without the receipt?'. The -도 is crucial: it implicitly acknowledges you know the receipt is normally required, which is more face-saving and polite than just asking as if the rule doesn't exist. Because Korean stores usually require 영수증, knowing alternatives is practically important: a card purchase (카드 결제) leaves a 카드 내역 (card transaction record) that can often substitute. The dividing line from 영수증 없으면 환불 안 돼요? is framing: 없이도 …돼요? hopefully asks 'can it still be done?', while 없으면 …안 돼요? pessimistically asks 'is it impossible without one?' — both are polite, 없이도 sounds more constructive. The English-speaker error is forming 'without' with a clunky negative clause like 영수증 안 가지고 환불돼요? — the clean adverb is 없이. Dropping -도 (영수증 없이 환불돼요?) is fine but slightly loses the 'even/acknowledging the norm' nuance.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 + 없이 ('without', adverb of 없다) + 도 ('even') + 환불돼요? → 'even without the receipt, is a refund possible?'. The -도 politely signals you know the receipt is normally required — you're asking about the exception, not ignoring the rule.

When you've lost the receipt or it was a gift. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Strengthen your case by mentioning your payment method: 카드로 샀어요, 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? — card records often substitute. Don't use 반말 with staff.
없이도 …돼요? (constructive: 'can it still be done?') vs 없으면 …안 돼요? (pessimistic: 'is it impossible?') vs 영수증 꼭 있어야 돼요? ('is the receipt absolutely required?'). All three are polite; choose based on tone.
없이도 환불돼요? → 없이도 교환돼요? → 없이도 반품돼요?. Add alternatives: 카드 내역으로 가능해요? ('is the card record enough?'), 앱 구매 내역으로 가능해요? ('can the app purchase history work?').

없이 (adverb: 'without') is the clean form — don't substitute 안 가지고 ('without bringing'). Dropping -도 gives 영수증 없이 환불돼요? which is fine but loses the face-saving 'even though I know it's needed' nuance that -도 carries.

mistakes: Saying 영수증 안 가지고 환불돼요? for 'without the receipt'.
That's clumsy. The clean way to say 'without' is the adverb 없이: 영수증 없이(도) 환불돼요?.
Confusing 없이 (without) with 없으면 (if there isn't).
없이 = 'without' (adverb); 없으면 = 'if there's none' (conditional). Both work but differ: 영수증 없이도 환불돼요? vs. 영수증 없으면 환불 안 돼요?.
Forgetting you paid by card.
A card purchase leaves a 카드 내역 that can stand in for the receipt. Mention 카드로 샀어요 — it often unlocks a refund even 영수증 없이.

english: I'd just like a refund (not an exchange)
usage: Polite; declining exchange, wanting money back
반말, to a friend or casual seller
A refund, not an exchange, please
교환 말고 ('not an exchange') makes the contrast explicit
Could I possibly get a refund?
examples: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요.
I'd just like a refund.
Said when staff offer an exchange but you want money back; 그냥 keeps the refusal gentle.
교환은 됐고요, 그냥 환불받고 싶어요.
Never mind the exchange — I'd just like a refund.
교환은 됐다 ('I'm done with the exchange [idea]') politely closes off the staff's alternative offer;됐다 here means 'no thanks, that's enough' not 'it worked'.
A: 교환해 드릴까요? / B: 아니요, 그냥 환불받고 싶어요. 교환 말고요.
A: Shall I arrange an exchange? / B: No, I'd just like a refund. Not an exchange.
B uses 그냥 + 교환 말고요 together — the double-emphasis politely but unmistakably insists on money, not a replacement.
nuance: 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 is 그냥 ('just/simply') + 환불받다 ('to receive a refund', 환불 + 받다 'receive') + 고 싶어요 ('want to'). The 그냥 does crucial social work: it signals 'just / never mind the alternatives', which is how you politely decline a pushy exchange offer without sounding aggressive. Korean staff often steer you toward 교환 (exchange) or store credit first, and 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 gently but firmly insists on money back. Note the giver/receiver verb distinction: 환불받다 (receive a refund, customer's perspective) vs 환불해 주다 / 환불하다 (issue a refund, staff's action); as the customer wanting your money returned, 환불받고 싶어요 is the natural form — 환불해 주고 싶어요 ('I want to give a refund') reverses the roles. The dividing line from bare 환불해 주세요 is softness: adding 그냥 frames it as 'I'd simply prefer a refund', de-escalating — useful when staff push back. For maximum clarity, combine: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요. The English-speaker error is omitting 그냥 and repeating a flat 환불해 주세요 under pressure, which can sound confrontational.

structuredNuance.t: 그냥 ('just, simply') + 환불받다 ('receive a refund') + 고 싶어요 ('want to'). 그냥 is the softener that says 'I'm not being difficult — I simply want my money back'. It de-escalates a potentially tense pushback.
Used when staff offer 교환 (exchange) or 적립금 (store credit) but you want cash/card credit back. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Appropriate with any staff. Combine with 교환 말고 for emphasis: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요.

그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (soft, declining alternatives) vs 환불해 주세요 (direct request, no implicit decline of alternatives) vs 교환 말고 환불해 주세요 (explicit contrast). 환불받다 (customer receives) ≠ 환불해 주다 (staff gives) — don't swap the verb.
그냥 환불받고 싶어요 → 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 → 적립금 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 (declining store credit). Softer: 그냥 환불받을 수 있을까요?

두 함정: (1) 환불해 주고 싶어요 reverses the roles — 해 주다 = 'give', so you'd be saying 'I want to give a refund'. Say 환불받고 싶어요 (receive). (2) Dropping 그냥 when declining an exchange makes 환불해 주세요 sound blunt under pressure; 그냥 keeps it gentle.

mistakes: Saying 환불해 주고 싶어요 to mean 'I want a refund'.
환불해 주다 is to GIVE a refund (the staff's action). As the customer receiving money, say 환불받고 싶어요.
Dropping 그냥 when declining an exchange.
Without 그냥, repeating 환불해 주세요 can sound blunt under pressure. 그냥 softens it to 'I'd simply prefer a refund' while staying firm.
Assuming a refund is automatic over an exchange.
Staff often push 교환 or store credit first. Be explicit: 교환 말고 그냥 환불받고 싶어요 ('not an exchange — just a refund').

usage: Polite; assuring staff the item wasn't used
반말, to a friend or casual seller
한 번도 ('not even once') for stronger emphasis
I didn't even open the packaging
포장 안 뜯다 ('didn't tear the wrapping'), the strongest proof
examples: 이거 안 쓴 거예요.
This is unused.
Reassuring staff during a return so they accept it; the adnominal construction describes the item's condition, not just your past action.
택도 안 뗐고 안 쓴 거예요.
The tag's still on and it's unused.
택 안 떼다 ('tag not removed') is physical, verifiable proof; stacking it with 안 쓴 거예요 makes a much stronger case.
A: 왜 반품하시려고요? / B: 선물 받았는데 저한테 안 맞아서요. 안 쓴 거예요.
A: Why do you want to return it? / B: I received it as a gift but it doesn't suit me. It's unused.
B's 선물 받았다 explains the absence of a receipt; 안 쓴 거예요 confirms the item's condition, which together is the best case for a gift return.
nuance: 안 쓴 거예요 is 안 ('not') + 쓴 (past adnominal of 쓰다 'to use') + 거예요 ('it is the thing that…'), literally 'it's a not-used thing' → 'it's unused'. 쓰다 here means 'to use' (쓰다 is polysemous: also 'to write', 'to wear glasses/hat', 'to be bitter' — context disambiguates; with a product it clearly means 'use'). This phrase matters because Korean return policies hinge on condition: 미개봉 (unopened packaging), 미사용 (unused), 택 그대로 (tag intact) all strengthen your claim. The dividing line: 안 쓴 거예요 is the everyday spoken form of the formal 미사용 (未使用) printed in policies; 포장 안 뜯었어요 ('packaging not opened') and 택 안 뗐어요 ('tag not removed') are even more concrete and persuasive. The English-speaker error is reaching for the perfect tense and saying 안 사용했어요 — that's fine as 'I didn't use it', but to DESCRIBE the item as unused, the adnominal form 안 쓴 거예요 is more native. The critical verb-confusion trap: 쓰다 'use' vs 사다 'buy' — 안 산 거예요 means 'something I didn't buy' (the opposite of helpful). Also, the past adnominal of 쓰다 is simply 쓴 (not 쓰은), so 안 쓴 거예요, never 안 쓰은 거예요.

structuredNuance.t: 안 + 쓴 (past adnominal of 쓰다 'use') + 거예요 ('it's the thing that…') → 'it's an unused thing'. The adnominal form describes the ITEM's condition, not just your past action — more natural than the plain-past 안 썼어요 in this context.

Essential to say during any return to confirm the item's condition. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Back it up with physical evidence: 택도 안 뗐어요 (tag on), 포장도 안 뜯었어요 (packaging sealed). Staff will often check before accepting.
안 쓴 거예요 (spoken, describes item) vs 미사용 제품이에요 (formal, label language) vs 한 번도 안 썼어요 (emphasizes how often: 'not even once'). Stack for impact: 포장도 안 뜯었고 안 쓴 거예요 ('packaging intact and unused').
안 쓴 거예요 → 한 번도 안 썼어요 → 포장도 안 뜯었어요 → 택도 안 뗐어요. Formal: 미사용 상태예요. The past adnominal is 쓴 (not 쓰은): 안 쓴 거예요.
두 함정: (1) 쓰다 'use' vs 사다 'buy' — 안 산 거예요 = 'something I didn't buy', not 'unused'. (2) Adnominal form: 쓰다 → 쓴 (not 쓰은). Say 안 쓴 거예요, never 안 쓰은 거예요.

mistakes: Saying 안 쓰은 거예요.
The past adnominal of 쓰다 is 쓴, not 쓰은. Say 안 쓴 거예요.
Confusing 쓰다 'use' with 사다 'buy'.
안 쓴 거 = unused; 안 산 거 = not bought. To say the item is unused, it's 안 쓴 거예요, not 안 산 거예요.
Thinking 'unused' alone guarantees a return.
Stores also check 택 (tag), 포장 (packaging), and time limits. Reinforce with 택도 안 뗐어요 / 포장도 안 뜯었어요 alongside 안 쓴 거예요.

english: I bought it not long ago
usage: I bought it not long ago
Polite; stressing the purchase was recent
반말, to a friend or casual seller
It's only been a few days
며칠 ('a few days') pins it down more
Naming the exact day, the most concrete version
examples: 이거 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
I bought this not long ago.
Establishing you're within the return window — the first thing staff mentally calculate when you walk in.
산 지 얼마 안 됐는데 벌써 고장 났어요.
I bought it recently and it's already broken.
벌써 ('already') highlights how premature the failure is, implying it's a quality issue, not normal wear.
A: 언제 구매하셨어요? / B: 산 지 일주일도 안 됐어요. 영수증도 있어요.
A: When did you buy it? / B: It hasn't even been a week. I have the receipt too.
B answers the staff's standard question precisely (일주일도 안 됐어요 = 'not even a week') and proactively adds 영수증도 있어요 — the two things staff always need.
nuance: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is 산 (past adnominal of 사다 'to buy') + 지 (bound noun marking elapsed time SINCE an action) + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much has become' → 'not long has passed'). The construction -ㄴ 지 + time + 되다 is the standard Korean way to say 'it's been [time] since I did X': 산 지 일주일 됐어요 = 'it's been a week since I bought it'. 얼마 안 됐어요 means 'not much time has passed', i.e. 'it was recent'. This is crucial to establish because refund/exchange eligibility depends on the purchase date, and staff will ask 언제 사셨어요? ('when did you buy it?'). The dividing line from 어제 샀어요 ('I bought it yesterday') is precision: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 is vaguer ('recently'), while naming the day is more concrete and convincing if you're close to the deadline. Two traps: the 지 marking elapsed time is written with a SPACE (산 지), unlike the connective -는지 ('whether', written attached: 샀는지); confusing them changes the meaning. Also: don't say 산 지 얼마 안 했어요 — time passing uses 되다, not 하다. And it must be the past adnominal 산 (not 사는 지, present), because the buying is complete.

structuredNuance.t: 산 (past adnominal of 사다) + 지 (elapsed-time noun) + 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not much time has become') → 'not long has passed since I bought it'. The -ㄴ 지 되다 construction is the standard 'it's been X time since' frame. Staff use this to assess whether you're in the return window.

Say this the moment you approach the counter — it's the first data point staff need. 해요체 (polite-neutral). If you know the exact date, name it (어제 산 거예요, 이틀 전에 샀어요) for a more convincing case. Pair with 영수증 여기 있어요 for maximum impact.
산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 (vague 'recently') vs 산 지 며칠 안 됐어요 ('only a few days') vs 어제 산 거예요 (exact day, most concrete). More precise is more persuasive when you're near the deadline.
-ㄴ 지 되다 with time: 산 지 일주일 됐어요 / 산 지 이틀 됐어요 / 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요. Stress: 산 지 일주일도 안 됐어요 ('not even a week'). The -도 adds 'not even', intensifying the recency claim.
두 함정: (1) 산지 (no space) vs 산 지 (space required — this 지 is a separate bound noun). 산지 merged is wrong. (2) 산 지 얼마 안 했어요 is wrong — elapsed-time uses 되다, not 하다: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요.

mistakes: Writing 산지 (no space) or confusing it with -는지.
The elapsed-time 지 is a separate bound noun, spaced: 산 지. The connective -는지 ('whether') is different: 샀는지 몰라요 means 'I don't know whether I bought it'.
Saying 산 지 얼마 안 했어요.
Time passing uses 되다, not 하다: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ('not long has passed'). 안 했어요 is wrong here.
Using the wrong tense: 사는 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
The purchase is finished, so use the past adnominal 산: 산 지 얼마 안 됐어요, not 사는 지.

english: It was already like this when I got it
usage: It was like this from when I got it
Polite; insisting the fault wasn't your doing
It was like this when I got it
반말, to a friend or casual seller
It was like this from the start
처음부터 ('from the beginning'), a simpler version
I'm not the one who did it
Stating directly that it wasn't your fault
examples: 이거 받았을 때부터 이랬어요.
It was already like this when I got it.
Defending against the implicit assumption you caused the damage — 받았을 때부터 pins the fault to before you ever touched it.
저 안 떨어뜨렸어요. 받았을 때부터 이랬어요. 사진도 있어요.
I didn't drop it — it was like this when I got it. I have photos too.
안 떨어뜨렸다 ('didn't drop it') heads off the most common counter-accusation; 사진도 있어요 offers the decisive evidence.
A: 이거 고객님이 사용하시다가 그러신 거 아닌가요? / B: 아니요, 박스 열자마자 봤는데 받았을 때부터 이랬어요.
A: Isn't this damage from how you used it? / B: No — I noticed it the moment I opened the box. It was like this when I got it.

This is the most realistic dispute scenario: A's 사용하시다가 그러신 거 아닌가요? is the staff deflection; B counters with 박스 열자마자 ('the instant I opened the box'), the strongest possible claim of pre-existing fault.
nuance: 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 is 받다 ('to receive/get') + -았을 때 ('at the time when [past action completed]') + 부터 ('from/since') + 이랬어요 (contracted past of 이렇다 'to be like this'). It means 'it was already like this from the very moment I received it'. This is the line you use when staff suspect you caused the damage and you need to insist the fault is pre-existing (not 사용자 과실, 'user's fault'). Proving it's pre-existing is what secures a free refund or exchange, as opposed to a repair cost being charged to you. 이랬어요 is the contracted spoken past of 이렇다 (이러했어요 → 이랬어요); attempting 이렇었어요 is wrong. The dividing line from 처음부터 이랬어요 ('it was like this from the beginning') is specificity: 받았을 때부터 pins it to the exact moment of receipt — especially powerful for online orders where there's a delivery record — while 처음부터 is a looser 'from the start'. The English-speaker error is tense mismatch: 받을 때 이래요 (present tense on both verbs) misses that both the receiving and the state are past. Another pitfall is the confrontational route of saying 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault') — stating facts (받았을 때부터 이랬어요) is calmer, harder to argue with, and more persuasive.

structuredNuance.t: 받았을 때 ('at the time I received it') + 부터 ('from/since') + 이랬어요 ('was like this'). 'From the very moment I got it, it was in this state.' 부터 anchors the fault before you, ruling out user damage — that's the legal/practical force of this phrase.

Used when staff challenge whether you caused the damage. 해요체 (polite-neutral). Point at the defect as you speak. Strengthen with 사진도 있어요 (unboxing photos) or 박스 열자마자 봤어요 ('I saw it the moment I opened the box'). Never drop to 반말 with staff, even under frustration.

받았을 때부터 이랬어요 (pinned to moment of receipt — strong for online delivery) vs 처음부터 이랬어요 ('from the beginning' — vaguer, works for any purchase) vs 제가 그런 거 아니에요 ('I didn't do it' — direct but confrontational). Factual > accusatory.

이랬어요 (contracted form, natural) — don't say 이렇었어요. Add evidence: 박스 열자마자 이랬어요 / 사진 찍어 뒀어요 ('I took photos'). For online orders: 배송받자마자 확인했는데 이랬어요 ('I checked as soon as it arrived and it was like this').

두 함정: (1) Tense — both the receiving and the state are past: 받았을 때 + 이랬어요, NOT 받을 때 이래요 (present). (2) 이랬어요 is the correct contracted past; 이렇었어요 is wrong. Also: 제 잘못 아니에요 is confrontational — stating facts is more persuasive.

mistakes: Saying 받을 때 이래요 (present tense).
Both the receiving and the condition are in the past: 받았을 때 ('when I received it') + 이랬어요 ('was like this'). Present tense misses that it was already faulty.
Trying to say 이랬어요 as 이렇었어요.
이렇다 contracts in the past to 이랬어요 (from 이러했어요), not 이렇었어요. Use 이랬어요.
Leading with 제 잘못 아니에요 ('it's not my fault').
That's confrontational. Stating the fact — 받았을 때부터 이랬어요 — makes the same point more calmly and is harder to argue with, especially with 사진 (photos).

usage: Polite; asking staff to carry out the refund
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Could you process the refund, please?
I'd appreciate it if you'd process the refund
Very polite/formal, useful in writing or to a manager
examples: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
Please process the refund.
Once the reason is accepted and the details are confirmed — this is the final execution step, asking them to push it through.
확인되셨으면 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
If you've confirmed everything, please process the refund.
확인되셨으면 ('if/once you've checked') acknowledges the staff's verification step and moves the conversation forward.
A: 네, 환불 가능하세요. 어떻게 해 드릴까요? / B: 카드 취소로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.
A: Yes, a refund is possible. How would you like to proceed? / B: Please process it as a card cancellation.
B specifies 카드 취소 (card cancellation) — the correct channel for card purchases — ensuring the staff process it to the right account.
nuance: 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 is 환불 ('refund') + 처리 ('processing/handling', Sino-Korean 處理) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). Adding 처리 makes it about completing the administrative action — running the card cancellation, logging the return in the system — rather than just the concept of a refund. This is the natural register at a service desk where the refund is a procedure. The 좀 cushions the request and is almost always present in spoken Korean requests. The dividing line from bare 환불해 주세요 is stage: 환불해 주세요 works at any point ('please refund me'), while 환불 처리를 해 주세요 specifically says 'please execute the refund now' — you use it once the reason is accepted. 처리 is productive and transfers: 교환 처리 (process the exchange), 취소 처리 (process the cancellation), A/S 처리 (handle after-sales service). The particle: it's 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요 — 처리 is the object of 하다 — not 환불 처리가 해 주세요. The English-speaker error is treating 처리 as optional formality and either over-formalizing in a tiny shop (where 환불해 주세요 is warmer) or being too casual at a department-store counter (where 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 fits better). Always state the refund method (카드 취소 / 현금).

structuredNuance.t: 환불 + 처리(處理, 'processing/handling') + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The addition of 처리 shifts the request from the concept of a refund to the execution of a procedure. Use it once everything is agreed — this is the 'now do it' step.

At a service desk or customer center once the refund eligibility is confirmed. 해요체 (polite-neutral). For a tiny market stall, 환불해 주세요 is warmer. For a department-store service desk or writing to customer service: 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 / 환불 처리해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.

환불 처리 해 주세요 (execute the refund now, procedural) vs 환불해 주세요 (general request, any stage). 처리 is productive: 교환 처리 (exchange), 취소 처리 (cancellation), 반품 처리 (return). Mention method: 카드 취소로 처리해 주세요 / 현금으로 처리해 주세요.
환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 → 환불 처리 좀 해 주시겠어요? → 환불 처리 부탁드려요 → 환불 처리해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (most formal/written). Add method: 카드 취소로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요.

두 함정: (1) 환불 처리가 해 주세요 is wrong — 처리 is the object: 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요. (2) Over-formalizing: in a casual market 처리 sounds stiff; save it for service desks. Also: always state the refund method (카드 취소 / 현금) so it's processed correctly.

mistakes: Saying 환불 처리가 해 주세요.
처리 is the object of 하다, so it takes 를 (often dropped), not 가: 환불 처리(를) 해 주세요.
Over-formalizing in a tiny shop.
At a small market stall, 환불 처리 부탁드립니다 can sound stiff. A warm 환불해 주세요 fits better; save 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 for service desks and counters.
Not stating the refund method.
Refunds go back by the original method (카드 결제 → 카드 취소). Say 카드 취소로 / 현금으로 환불 처리 좀 해 주세요 so it's done correctly.

english: So you're saying this can't be refunded?
usage: Polite; pushing back / confirming a refusal
반말, to a friend or casual seller
Do you mean it can't be refunded?
examples: 네? 이거 환불이 안 된다고요?
Sorry? This can't be refunded?
네? (rising intonation: 'sorry?') + the echo signals genuine surprise; it politely forces the staff to re-explain rather than simply accepting the refusal.
불량인데도 환불이 안 된다고요?
Even though it's defective, it can't be refunded?
불량인데도 ('even though it's defective') names the concrete reason why the refusal seems unreasonable; this kind of pushback often prompts a manager referral.
A: 세일 상품은 환불이 안 됩니다. / B: 그럼 교환은 되는데 환불이 안 된다고요?
A: Sale items cannot be refunded. / B: So an exchange is fine but no refund?
B doesn't argue with the policy directly but clarifies the exact scope of the refusal — this is a smart pivot that often reveals an exchange option you hadn't been offered.
nuance: 이거 환불이 안 된다고요? is 이거 ('this') + 환불이 안 되다 ('a refund isn't possible') + -다고요? (a quotative ending that echoes back the other person's statement with rising intonation). The -다고요? is the core of this phrase: it repeats what was just said to confirm or gently challenge it — 'you're telling me…?' — and is the polite, non-aggressive way to push back when a store refuses. The rising intonation signals surprise/disbelief without accusation, which often prompts staff to re-explain or escalate to a manager. The dividing line from 왜 안 돼요? ('why not?') is tone: 안 된다고요? mirrors their own words and sounds like incredulous confirmation rather than a demand, keeping the exchange civil while making clear you're not satisfied. To go fully polite (e.g. to a manager), use 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? ('are you saying it can't be refunded?', with honorific 말씀). The English-speaker error is dropping the quotative and saying 환불 안 돼요? again — that just re-asks the yes/no question and loses the 'wait, are you telling me that…' pushback force. The final 요 is non-negotiable: 환불 안 된다고? without 요 is 반말 and sounds confrontational or rude to staff. Particle: 환불이 안 돼요 (subject 이/가), never 환불을.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 + 환불이 안 된다 ('a refund is not possible') + -고요? (quotative echo, rising). Literally: 'you're saying a refund is not possible for this?' The -다고요? is a polite echo-back frame, not a new question — it signals surprise and invites re-explanation or escalation.

When staff refuse a refund and you want to push back without escalating. 해요체 (polite-neutral) — the 요 is essential. Upgrade to 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? (honorific 말씀) when addressing a manager. Never drop to 반말 with staff even under frustration.

-다고요? (echo-back, polite disbelief/confirmation) vs 왜 안 돼요? (direct demand for reason) vs 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? (fully honorific version). -다고요? is the most tactically useful: it keeps tone calm while clearly not accepting the refusal.
-다고요? is versatile: 교환도 안 된다고요? / 영수증 있어도 안 된다고요?. Escalate: 환불이 안 된다는 말씀이세요? → 담당자분을 불러 주시겠어요? ('could you get the person in charge?'). Always include 요 with staff.

두 함정: (1) Re-asking 환불 안 돼요? just restates the question — it loses the 'wait, are you telling me that…' pushback force of -다고요?. (2) Dropping 요: 환불 안 된다고? (no 요) is 반말 and rude to staff. Always keep 요.

mistakes: Re-asking 환불 안 돼요? instead of echoing.
That just repeats the plain question. To push back / confirm a refusal, use the quotative echo: 환불이 안 된다고요? ('you're saying it can't be refunded?').
Dropping the 요: 환불 안 된다고?.
Without the final 요, -다고 is 반말 and sounds curt or confrontational to staff. Keep it polite: 환불이 안 된다고요?.
Using 환불을 안 돼요.
되다 takes the subject particle: 환불이 안 돼요 / 환불이 안 된다고요?. 환불을 is wrong with 되다.
